content: An endometrial biopsy is a medical procedure in which a small sample of tissue is taken from the lining of the uterus, known as the endometrium. This tissue is then examined under a microscope to identify any abnormal cells or signs of cancer. The procedure can be performed with or without anesthesia. During the biopsy, the patient lies on their back with their feet in stirrups. The healthcare provider conducts a pelvic examination and inserts a speculum into the vagina to hold it open and visualize the cervix. The cervix is cleaned with an antiseptic solution and stabilized using an instrument called a tenaculum. If the cervical canal is tight (a condition known as stenosis), a cervical dilator may be used to gently stretch it. A small, hollow plastic tube is then inserted into the uterine cavity, and gentle suction is applied to collect a sample of the endometrial lining. Once the sample is obtained, the instruments are removed, and the tissue is sent to a pathologist for microscopic examination. Endometrial biopsy is typically performed to investigate the cause of abnormal menstrual bleeding, such as heavy, prolonged, or irregular periods, bleeding after menopause, or bleeding associated with hormone therapy. It may also be done if a thickened uterine lining is observed on ultrasound. This test is most commonly performed in women over the age of 35 and can also be used to screen for endometrial cancer. Additionally, it may be part of the diagnostic process for women experiencing infertility, as it can help determine if the endometrial lining is responding appropriately to hormonal stimulation to support implantation of a fertilized egg. No special preparation is required for an endometrial biopsy. However, patients may choose to take ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin IB) or acetaminophen (Tylenol) about an hour before the procedure to help reduce cramping. During the procedure, the instruments may feel cold, and some discomfort or pain may occur when the cervix is grasped. Cramping is also common as the instruments enter the uterus and the tissue sample is collected. Endometrial biopsies are performed in hospitals or specialized medical centers. Patients can consult their healthcare provider for directions to facilities that offer this procedure. Possible complications of an endometrial biopsy include infection, uterine perforation or cervical tearing (though these are rare), prolonged bleeding, and mild spotting. The results of the biopsy can be classified as normal or abnormal. A normal result indicates that the cells in the sample show no abnormalities. Abnormal results may reveal conditions such as endometrial cancer or precancerous changes (hyperplasia), uterine fibroids, uterine polyps, or hormone imbalances. If the biopsy is conducted as part of an infertility evaluation, the sample can help determine whether the endometrial lining is being properly stimulated by hormones to support implantation of a fertilized egg.
